name: DementiaBench: home safety for a person living with dementia
description: Visually detectable home hazards for a person living with dementia at home. Wording is original; each hazard cites the guideline line it comes from. Types: object (something present that should not be), access (something that enables an unsafe activity: driving, leaving), perception (a feature that is misread because of dementia-related perceptual change: dark mat as hole, reflection as stranger, low contrast). Not clinically validated; requires OT review.

severity_scale.high: Could cause serious injury, poisoning, fire, or getting lost if left for one day.
severity_scale.medium: Raises risk of falls, distress or confusion; fix within days.

style: Photorealistic smartphone photo taken at eye level in a modest, lived-in American home of an 80-year-old. Natural light, realistic everyday objects, no people, no text.

Patients go home on a walker. The house decides whether they fall.
To someone with dementia, a dark mat is a hole and a mirror is a stranger.

1 in 3

joint-replacement patients fall within a year of surgery.

6 in 10

people living with dementia will wander at least once (Alzheimer's Association).

~31%

of falls are caused by the environment — rugs, missing grab bars, low toilets.

Same

object, different hazard: a rug is a trip risk for a walker user, but a hole or step to someone whose depth perception has changed (NIA, Alzheimer's Society).

15

hazards, each citing a line of the guidance: stove, sharps, pills, chemicals, firearms, car keys, open doors, mirrors, dark mats, bold patterns.
Start from the post-op fall-prevention guideline (CDC STEADI, HOME FAST, SAFER-HOME).
Start from dementia home-safety guidance (Alzheimer's Association checklist, NIA, Alzheimer's Society, HEAP).

Object = something in the way (rug, cord, clutter). Absence = something missing (grab bar, stair rail). Measurement = geometry (toilet height, doorway too narrow for a walker). Lighting = too dark to see the path.

Object = something dangerous within reach (pills, knives, bleach, a heater against bedding). Access / wandering = something that enables an unsafe activity (car keys by the door, an open front door). Misperception = a normal object that dementia makes dangerous (a dark mat read as a hole, a bold rug read as steps, a mirror read as an intruder).
Models see objects. They can't judge whether they're safe.
Models see objects. They can't see them the way the patient does.

hazards.name: Stove burner left on, knobs freely usable
hazards.visual_description: A gas stovetop burner is lit with a visible blue flame and nothing on it (or an empty pan), and the stove knobs are bare with no knob covers.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Forgetting a lit burner and misjudging heat are core dementia fire/burn risks; a person may turn knobs on repeatedly. Fix: knob covers, automatic shut-off device, or disconnect the stove.

citation.guideline_line: Use stove knob covers or remove knobs, shut off gas when not cooking, prefer appliances with automatic shut-off.

render.inpaint: the top of an electric stove with a spiral burner coil glowing bright red-orange hot

hazards.name: Knives and sharps out on the counter
hazards.visual_description: A wooden knife block full of large kitchen knives and a loose chef's knife lie on the open counter within easy reach.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Judgment about sharp objects declines; knives should be locked away rather than left in the open.

citation.guideline_line: Lock up or remove knives, scissors and other sharp items.

render.inpaint: a wooden knife block full of large kitchen knives and a big chef's knife lying loose on the countertop

hazards.name: Cleaning chemicals out and unlocked
hazards.visual_description: A bottle of bleach, a spray cleaner and a clear tub of colorful laundry detergent pods sit on the counter next to the sink.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Colorful pods and bottles can be mistaken for food or drink by a person with dementia (ingestion/poisoning).

citation.guideline_line: Keep bleach and laundry pods out of sight, secured, in original containers so they are not swallowed.

render.inpaint: a white bleach jug, a blue spray cleaner bottle and a clear tub of colorful laundry detergent pods on the countertop

hazards.name: Medication bottles left out
hazards.visual_description: Several orange prescription pill bottles and an open weekly pill organizer sit on the kitchen counter.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Unsupervised access risks double-dosing or skipped doses; medications should be locked and dispensed by a caregiver.

citation.guideline_line: Clear prescription drugs and vitamins off counters and tables; lock medications away.

render.inpaint: several orange prescription pill bottles and an open weekly pill organizer on the countertop

hazards.name: Razor and medications out on the sink
hazards.visual_description: A disposable razor, a straight razor-style blade and two prescription pill bottles sit out on the bathroom sink counter.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Sharps and medications in the bathroom are a common unsupervised-access point.

citation.guideline_line: Lock away medicines and sharp items (razors) in the bathroom.

render.inpaint: a razor blade and two orange prescription pill bottles lying on the bathroom sink counter

hazards.name: White toilet seat on white toilet and floor (low contrast)
hazards.visual_description: The toilet seat and lid are plain white, matching a white toilet against a white floor and white wall, so the seat blends into its surroundings.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Reduced contrast sensitivity makes a white-on-white toilet hard to locate; a colored seat helps with toileting and sitting safely.

citation.guideline_line: Choose a toilet seat and fittings that contrast with wall and floor so they can be found.

hazards.render_note: Not rendered in v0: every reused bathroom base already has a white seat on a white toilet, so this hazard would be present in the clean base.

hazards.name: Dark bath mat on a light floor
hazards.visual_description: A solid black bath mat lies on the light tile floor in front of the toilet/tub.
hazards.dementia_modifier: A dark mat can be perceived as a hole or step by someone with dementia, causing freezing, stepping over, or falls.

citation.guideline_line: Dark rugs and mats can look like obstacles or holes in the floor.

render.inpaint: a solid black bath mat lying on the light tile floor

hazards.name: Plugged-in hair dryer by the sink
hazards.visual_description: A hair dryer is plugged into the wall outlet and lying on the counter right beside the filled sink basin.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Electrical appliances near water are a shock risk when judgment is impaired.

citation.guideline_line: Remove small electrical appliances from the bathroom and cover outlets.

render.inpaint: a black hair dryer plugged into the wall outlet with its cord, lying on the counter right next to the sink basin

hazards.name: Large mirror facing the bed
hazards.visual_description: A large full-length mirror stands on the wall directly facing the bed, clearly reflecting the bed.
hazards.dementia_modifier: A person with dementia may not recognize their own reflection and think a stranger is in the room, causing fear or agitation.

citation.guideline_line: Use fewer, smaller, carefully placed mirrors; reflections can confuse (Alzheimer's Society: remove or cover them).

render.inpaint: a large rectangular wall mirror hanging on the wall, clearly reflecting the bedroom and the bed

hazards.name: Bold high-contrast patterned rug
hazards.visual_description: A large rug with a bold black-and-white geometric or striped pattern covers the floor beside the bed.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Busy patterns can be misread as steps, objects or holes, causing hesitation, reaching for things that are not there, or falls.

citation.guideline_line: Avoid busy patterns; a change in floor pattern can be mistaken for a step because depth perception changes.

render.inpaint: a large area rug with a bold black-and-white zigzag geometric pattern on the carpet

hazards.name: Space heater next to bedding
hazards.visual_description: A portable electric space heater, switched on with glowing coils, stands on the floor touching the hanging bedspread.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Portable heaters near fabric are a fire and burn risk that a person with dementia may not recognize.

render.inpaint: a portable electric space heater with glowing orange coils standing on the floor touching the hanging bedspread

hazards.name: Car keys hanging by the front door
hazards.visual_description: A set of car keys with a car fob hangs on a hook right next to the front door.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Visible car keys invite unsafe driving once driving has stopped; keys should be kept out of sight.

citation.guideline_line: Remove access to car keys once the person no longer drives.

render.inpaint: a small wall hook beside the front door with a car key and car remote fob hanging from it

hazards.name: Front door left open to the outside
hazards.visual_description: The front door stands wide open showing the porch and street outside.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Six in ten people with dementia will wander; an unsecured, open exit is the main wandering pathway.

citation.guideline_line: Most people with dementia will wander; secure exterior doors (deadbolts out of eye line), disguise exits or add door alerts.

render.inpaint: the front door standing wide open, showing the sunny porch and street outside

hazards.name: Clutter piles in the walkway
hazards.visual_description: Stacks of newspapers, boxes and shoes are piled on the floor along the hallway walking path.
hazards.dementia_modifier: Clutter increases falls and confusion; visual crowding makes navigation harder for people with dementia.

citation.guideline_line: Remove throw rugs, cords and extra clutter; keep floors clear.

render.inpaint: piles of stacked newspapers, cardboard boxes and shoes on the floor in the walkway

bases_note: Base rooms are reused from HomeBench (data/renders/*, already photoreal older-adult homes). Edits are local inpaints inside a per-hazard mask (0-1000 coords), so everything outside the mask is pixel-identical to the base.
